title: Priority-handshake-prefill-eviction-exploratory-notes
content:
Summary:

This is a working note capturing a set of small-scale experiments that decouple two behaviors we've historically entangled in the continuous batcher: (1) prefill eviction (how aggressively we drop requests that are old or would cause batch prefill to exceed a token budget) and (2) the priority handshake / demotion window (how long a high-urgency request keeps its priority headroom when coalescing). The goal was to see if separating these concerns reduces 95/99 tail latency for mixed-tenant workloads while preserving fairness for low-priority tenants.

Motivation / background:
- Observed recurring tail spikes during microbursts where a high-priority stream repeatedly preempts low-priority requests.
- Our current implementation performs eviction decisions inside the same codepath that manages priority handshake state; traces suggest a coupling where an aggressive handshake grace period indirectly increases the prefill backlog and causes larger coalesced batches that occasionally exceed kernel optimal sizes.
- Hypothesis: treating "eviction aggressiveness" and "handshake persistence" as independent knobs will allow us to trade slightly higher small-batch overhead for much lower worst-case latency for mid-priority tenants.

Experiment design:
- Testbed: single-cluster simulator + small canary pool (4xA100 equiv nodes) replaying production inter-arrival and length distributions sampled from last week.
- Workload mix: 60% medium-latency interactive (priority=normal, median tokens=150), 25% high-urgency chat (priority=high, median tokens=60, bursty), 15% background embedder (priority=low, median tokens=512).
- Metrics collected: p50/p95/p99 latency (end-to-end), kernel token throughput (tokens/sec), batch size distribution, fairness index (Jain's index per-priority on latency), prefill-eviction rate, handshake re-promotions, CPU/GPU utilization, and KV cache hit delta.

Parameters swept:
- prefill_eviction_threshold_pct: [60, 70, 80, 90]  // fraction of batch token budget above which we start rejecting prefill candidates
- handshake_grace_ms: [10, 30, 75, 150]  // how long to keep priority promotion for an incoming urgent request
- priority_demote_window_s: [0.5, 2, 8]  // time after which promoted priority decays to baseline if not renewed
- batch_token_budget: fixed at 4096 tokens per GPU for this sweep (matching prod default)

Quick runbook note: each cell ran for 30 minutes steady-state after a 10 min warmup. We replayed the same trace 3x per cell and aggregated.

Key observations (high level):
- The most consistent wins for p99 on normal-priority tenants came from pairing a relatively conservative eviction threshold (80%) with a *short* handshake grace (30ms) and moderate demote window (2s).
- Extremely short handshake_grace_ms (10ms) reduced p99 for normal but increased error rate for high-priority chat requests due to lost handshake promotions (they ended up pushed into later batches and sometimes retried).
- Very long handshake_grace_ms (150ms) lowered p50 significantly for high-priority traffic but amplified p99 for low/normal tenants — consistent with a starvation effect where promoted requests hold slots that otherwise could have been used by queued lower-priority items.
- Lower eviction thresholds (60-70%) reduced the maximum batch size variance but increased the rate of outright rejects for large background requests, which raised retry overhead for background embedder flows. That said, because embeds are low priority, the end-user impact was small but billing and GPU throughput dropped.

Representative numbers (aggregated across runs; baseline = current prod knobs: eviction=70%, handshake=75ms, demote=8s):
- Baseline p99 (normal): 420ms
- Best cell found (eviction=80%, handshake=30ms, demote=2s):
  - p50 normal: 48ms (baseline 45ms)
  - p95 normal: 150ms (baseline 180ms)
  - p99 normal: 280ms (baseline 420ms)  <-- large improvement
  - p99 high: 120ms (baseline 90ms)  <-- small regression for high-priority
  - Embed throughput: -9% (more evictions/retries)
  - Fairness index (Jain) across priorities on p95 latency: 0.88 (baseline 0.74)  <-- improved fairness

Microtrace pattern notes:
- With handshake=75ms we saw chains of ~3 rapid high-priority arrivals that held a slot for >100ms in between coalesce cycles; when the chain stops, the leftover slot was filled with long-embed requests and produced enormous batches that raised kernel scheduling tails.
- With handshake=30ms the chains were shorter; the batcher still allowed urgent requests to coalesce but didn't reserve capacity long enough to prevent lower-priority items from entering the next immediate batch.

EV vs handshake decoupling behavior (qualitative):
- When eviction threshold was high (90%), we allowed large prefill accumulation; the batch size mode shifted from ~32 requests to ~48 in bursts, which increased amortized tokens per kernel call but produced higher tail due to stragglers (requests that contributed large token counts).
- Medium threshold (80%) hits a good sweet spot: avoids pathological huge batches but keeps enough headroom to service background work without unnecessary eviction.

Operational considerations / caveats:
- KV cache interplay: increased eviction leads to more cold cache executions for embed flows; measurable drop in cache-hit ratio (~4–7%) for embed requests at 80% eviction vs 70% baseline. Need to weigh cost/latency tradeoff for customers that heavily rely on embeddings.
- Retry amplification: embeds that are evicted often retry with backoff; we saw a small bump in total token count (3–6%) due to retries at 80% eviction. This can inflate costs for customers with high embed volumes.
- Observability: existing dashboards don't clearly show "handshake hold-time" metric; we should add a trace-level annotation to capture handshake start/expiry and correlate with batch composition.

Small experiments / reproducible trace snippets:
- Repro script: scripts/replays/prefill-handshake-sweep.py (see linked PR) — parameterized by the 3 knobs above.
- Example microtrace (cut):
  T=0ms: high-pri A arrives -> promoted, handshake starts
  T=10ms: normal B arrives -> queued, candidate for next batch
  T=20ms: high-pri C arrives -> handshake still active, A/C coalesce into same batch if handshake>20ms
  T=75ms: with handshake=75ms, promotion still active -> normal B gets delayed to later batch and may be coalesced with heavy embed E leading to long kernel op
  T=30ms: with handshake=30ms, promotion expires -> B allowed into earlier batch -> p99 improves for B-class

Recommendations (next steps):
1) Canary the pair (eviction=80%, handshake=30ms, demote=2s) in a low-risk shard focused on mixed-interactive workloads for 2 weeks with 10% traffic. Monitor p99 by tenant and embed throughput/cost.
2) Add observability hooks: handshake_start, handshake_expiry, eviction_reason tag on traces; add a small dashboard showing handshake_holding_count over time.
3) Add a safety gate: if embed-heavy tenants exceed X% billing delta due to evictions, bias knobs back (or add per-tenant prefill policies).
4) Explore a soft-eviction mode where we demote large low-priority requests to batch-incrementally (split large embed into two batchable chunks) rather than full reject. Could reduce retry amplification.
5) Run a longer-duration synthetic test (24h) with changing arrival patterns to validate against diurnal burstiness.

Open questions / TODOs:
- What's the right demote window for long-running conversational sessions with low churn? 2s worked well here, but sessions with frequent small messages might prefer 8s. We should segment by session length.
- Can we make handshake grace adaptive (shorten when queue depth exceeds threshold)? Initial simulation suggests adaptive handshake gives ~10% extra p99 improvement without harming high-pri p50, but we need production-safe rollout logic.
- How do we expose per-tenant preferences so enterprise customers with heavy embeddings can request a higher prefill budget? Need product input.

Notes to self:
- Re-run the best cell with batch_token_budget=8192 and quantify kernel-level scaling (some of the tail behavior may be kernel scheduling artifacts at larger budgets).
- Add a small feature flag to allow per-route eviction tuning; instrument impact on cost; coordinate with product before wide rollout.

Appendix: quick raw numbers for best cell (median across runs):
- p50 normal: 48ms
- p95 normal: 150ms
- p99 normal: 280ms
- p50 high: 30ms
- p95 high: 65ms
- p99 high: 120ms
- embed success rate (first try): 91% (baseline 98%)
- tokens/sec per GPU: 112k (baseline 123k)
- prefill_eviction_rate: 4.8% (baseline 2.1%)

If reviewers want, I can convert this into a short runbook for the canary and produce the replay artifacts + dashboards in next pass.

-- Aisha
